description: I’m Bhavit, a developer working on the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge. Looking for teammates interested in UI/UX design, data visualization, or video editing/storytelling to help build a clean interface and compelling demo.
summary:
Healthcare depends on recognizing emergencies and reaching medical professionals in time. For astronauts traveling to Mars, where communication delays reach 22 minutes one-way, this becomes a mission-critical vulnerability. On Earth, similar challenges affect millions facing falls, delayed diagnoses, and limited medical access.

HELM reimagines healthcare as autonomous, predictive infrastructure rather than passive monitoring.

Built independently, HELM combines personalized physiological intelligence, multi-signal threat detection, and predictive digital twins to identify deterioration before danger thresholds are crossed. Contactless camera sensing enables pulse estimation and potential emergency detection without specialized wearables. Offline decision support provides guidance when connectivity disappears.

Its defining innovation is verifiable autonomy: SHA-256-linked medical records, explainable alerts, and reproducible validation. Across 720 simulated normal observations and 90 injected emergencies, HELM reports 100% detection under tested conditions with fewer than 5% false alarms. Its computer-vision architecture builds on the developer's PubMed-indexed research.

Engineered for deep space, HELM pioneers an architecture for accessible, accountable health intelligence across spacecraft, rural healthcare, eldercare, disaster response, and underserved communities worldwide.
details:
A medical emergency should not become fatal simply because nobody noticed it in time, or because a doctor was too far away to help.

That is the problem HELM is built to address.

On a long-duration space mission, the human body faces risks that are difficult to manage even with medical supervision. According to NASA, astronauts can lose approximately 1–1.5% of bone density per month in weight-bearing bones during four-to-six-month missions. Approximately 70% of astronauts aboard the International Space Station experience swelling in the back of their eyes. A 2026 expert consensus study found that 81% of 64 evaluated NASA astronauts had at least one ocular finding associated with spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). These are not minor inconveniences: they demonstrate how spaceflight can progressively change the body, sometimes before obvious symptoms appear.

The challenge becomes even greater beyond Earth. NASA estimates that communication with a Mars crew can take up to approximately 22 minutes one way, meaning a simple question and response can require 44 minutes before accounting for medical evaluation and data transmission. Certain mission trajectories may also experience communication blackouts lasting days or weeks. A crew cannot depend on receiving immediate medical instructions from Earth.

HELM is designed to give astronauts an onboard system that monitors their health, identifies dangerous changes, recognizes possible emergencies, and helps them decide what to do next without depending on continuous internet access.

But this problem is much larger than space exploration.

On Earth, the CDC reports that more than 14 million Americans aged 65 and older fall every year. Falls are the leading cause of injury among older adults, and approximately 38,742 older adults died from falls in 2021. The estimated annual U.S. medical cost of nonfatal older-adult falls was $80 billion in 2020, including $57 billion paid by Medicare and Medicaid.

This is not a problem that the healthcare system is ignoring. Medicare already pays for remote patient monitoring, with payments exceeding $500 million in 2024, according to a 2025 federal oversight report. CMS has also launched the eight-year GUIDE dementia-care model, which began in 2024 and supports coordinated care, around-the-clock access to assistance, and caregiver respite services.

These initiatives demonstrate growing public investment in monitoring vulnerable patients and reducing preventable medical complications. However, Medicare remote-monitoring reimbursement is not the same as a dedicated fall-detection program, and GUIDE does not establish that HELM's particular technology is reimbursable.

HELM targets an important gap: collecting health data is only the first step. The next challenge is recognizing deterioration, responding to emergencies, and making information useful when a clinician cannot respond immediately.

HELM combines personalized health baselines, multi-signal detection, early-warning forecasting, camera-based pulse estimation, possible fall and unresponsive-person monitoring, and an auditable medical-event history in one offline-first system.

Its goal is to move health monitoring from simply displaying measurements toward providing timely, explainable decision support.

How it works

1. Personalized baselines — detecting changes before they become obvious

Traditional health monitoring often relies on broad population thresholds. But a normal reading for one person may be unusual for another, especially in microgravity, where the body adapts to a completely different environment.

HELM establishes an individual baseline using resting heart rate, blood pressure, heart-rate variability, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, sleep, mood, and reaction time. Instead of checking only whether a measurement falls outside a standard range, it also measures how far that reading has moved from the person's own history.

The interface displays both a personal reference band and a typical Earth reference range, allowing users to see when a measurement is unusual for them even if it still looks normal according to general population values.

This matters for both astronauts and people on Earth. An astronaut's cardiovascular measurements can change during adaptation to microgravity. An older adult recovering from illness may also experience a gradual change in resting physiology before developing more obvious symptoms.

HELM's advantage is individualized change detection, rather than assuming that one threshold fits everyone.

2. Multi-signal detection — connecting warning signs instead of treating them separately

A single elevated heart-rate measurement does not necessarily mean someone is sick. But a rising heart rate combined with falling heart-rate variability, higher temperature, and worsening sleep may warrant closer attention.

HELM evaluates combinations of measurements across six modeled problem classes: infection, elevated cabin carbon dioxide, radiation-related risk, sleep crisis, isolation-related mood decline, and cardiovascular strain.

The need for earlier recognition is substantial. According to the CDC, approximately 1.7 million U.S. adults develop sepsis each year, and at least 350,000 die in the hospital or are discharged to hospice. Most cases begin before hospital admission, illustrating why recognizing deterioration outside traditional clinical settings matters.

HELM's pattern engine is intended to flag concerning combinations and explain why they deserve attention. It does not claim to diagnose sepsis or replace medical testing. Instead, it provides an interpretable warning that could help users seek appropriate medical evaluation sooner.

The same approach is relevant in spacecraft, rural communities, disaster-response settings, and other environments where symptoms may develop long before a clinician can assess them.

3. Early-warning forecasting — detecting where health is heading

Most conventional dashboards describe the present. HELM also estimates the direction of change.

Its forecasting engine uses Theil–Sen robust regression to examine recent measurements, estimate their trend, and project whether a value may leave its personalized reference range within the next 14 days.

For example, HELM might display:

"Your resting heart rate is trending upward. At the current estimated rate, it could leave your personal reference range in approximately five days."

This is a trend projection, not a confirmed medical event or a clinically validated prediction of illness.

The forecast also appears in HELM's digital twin: an interactive body map showing monitored physiological systems, current warning states, and projected changes.

This is particularly relevant to long-duration missions. NASA identifies progressive bone loss, cardiovascular adaptation, neuro-ocular changes, and behavioral health as important spaceflight risks. Although HELM cannot directly measure bone density or diagnose SANS using its existing vital-sign channels, its longitudinal monitoring architecture could support a broader system that integrates specialized measurements in the future.

The goal is to give users more time to investigate changes, adjust approved countermeasures, and request medical assistance before deterioration becomes an emergency.

4. CameraPulse and possible fall detection — identifying emergencies without specialized wearable hardware

Falls are one of the clearest examples of why passive monitoring matters.

The CDC reports that more than one in four older Americans experience a fall each year. The age-adjusted fall death rate increased by 21% between 2018 and 2024, showing that this is not simply a historical problem.

HELM explores a low-cost alternative to monitoring systems that depend entirely on dedicated wearable devices.

Its CameraPulse module uses remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), analyzing subtle changes in facial skin color captured by a standard webcam to estimate pulse without physical contact.

Its unattended-monitoring mode also tracks whether repeated attempts to obtain a usable signal have failed. When that occurs, the system can flag a possible unresponsive person and initiate its configured notification workflow.

The fall and unresponsive-person detection work builds on the creator's earlier peer-reviewed research in computer vision and real-time monitoring.

In 2025, the creator was lead author of Real-Time Monitoring of Personal Protective Equipment Compliance Using Generative Artificial Intelligence and Computer Vision, published in Cureus and indexed in PubMed (DOI: 10.7759/cureus.95182).

That earlier system used Google Gemini, OpenCV, and Raspberry Pi hardware, achieving:

  • 95.8% accuracy across 168 controlled trials
  • 91.0% recall
  • 100% specificity
  • F1 score of 0.953
  • Cohen's Kappa of 0.916

Those results establish experience building and evaluating a real-time computer-vision monitoring system. They do not establish the clinical performance of HELM's fall detector.

HELM's adapted detection engine has separately reported approximately 94% accuracy across more than 100 self-tested trials. This remains preliminary internal evidence rather than independent clinical validation.

Importantly, a missing camera pulse signal does not prove unconsciousness, and a webcam cannot reliably observe a person outside its field of view. Lighting, motion, camera positioning, and environmental conditions can all interfere. HELM therefore treats these signals as potential warning indicators, not definitive diagnoses.

The longer-term opportunity is affordable, privacy-conscious emergency monitoring using hardware people may already own. That could be relevant to assisted-living facilities, home care, isolated work environments, and future space habitats, provided the technology passes appropriate real-world safety testing.

5. Symptom Checker and Care Plan — translating measurements into understandable guidance

Health measurements are useful only when people understand what they mean.

HELM allows an astronaut to describe symptoms in everyday language. Its deterministic clinical-pattern matcher connects the description with modeled physiological patterns, updates the demonstration scenario, and produces a structured care-plan response.

The system also presents exercise, nutrition, and other countermeasure information informed by NASA Human Research Program guidance.

This matters because long-duration missions require crews to operate with greater medical independence. NASA identifies distance from Earth as a major human-spaceflight hazard, particularly when medical emergencies occur and ground support is delayed.

HELM aims to reduce the time required to organize relevant information and identify an appropriate next step.

Its generated guidance is intended as educational and operational decision support, not independently authorized treatment. Any use for real astronauts or patients would require clinically reviewed protocols, defined escalation rules, and appropriate human oversight.

6. Offline medical decision support — built for when communication fails

A medical system that depends on cloud connectivity cannot be the sole source of support during a communication blackout.

NASA's Mars communication research describes one-way delays reaching approximately 22 minutes, along with the possibility of extended disruptions. A 2025 NASA technical presentation also notes that remote expert consultation can stretch the time required to reach a clinical decision into hours.

HELM is designed around that limitation.

Its core monitoring, pattern detection, forecasting, and local decision-support functions can operate without continuous internet access. The interface incorporates mission communication delay and helps organize information for onboard assessment or consultation.

It also generates structured SBAR reports: Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation. This gives crews a consistent format for communicating what happened, what measurements changed, and what assistance may be needed.

The same design principle applies to Earth-based environments with limited connectivity, including rural communities, submarines, polar stations, and disaster-response operations.

HELM's goal is to preserve useful health intelligence even when the network disappears.

7. Tamper-evident medical records — making every decision traceable

Trust is a major challenge in healthcare technology. If a system generates an alert, users should be able to understand which measurements triggered it and whether the recorded history has been altered.

HELM addresses record integrity with a SHA-256 hash-chain ledger.

Every event is linked cryptographically to the preceding event. If an earlier entry is changed without rebuilding the chain, subsequent verification can detect the inconsistency.

This creates a transparent record of readings, alerts, and system decisions.

The need for better protection of medical information is clear. According to HHS, 663 large healthcare-data breaches occurring in 2024 affected approximately 242.9 million reported individual records or individuals, with hacking and IT incidents accounting for the vast majority.

HELM's local-first approach reduces the need to transmit raw monitoring data to remote services. Its CameraPulse implementation processes facial color information locally rather than recording or uploading full video.

The hash chain adds tamper evidence, although it is not a substitute for encryption, authentication, secure backups, or external verification. Those safeguards would be necessary for clinical deployment.

The broader design principle is straightforward: a trustworthy health system should make its decisions understandable and its records independently checkable.

8. Live validation — showing how the system performs

HELM does not rely exclusively on static accuracy claims.

Its validation interface allows users to execute simulated mission scenarios directly in their browser using the same core detection functions employed by the application.

The supplied implementation includes 103 automated tests and a simulation workflow covering 30 missions, 720 calm-day checks, and 90 injected emergency events per validation run.

Under the specified simulated conditions, the project reports a false-alarm rate below 5% and detection of all injected emergencies.

These results are reproducible within the simulator, but they do not establish a 100% real-world emergency detection rate or a clinically validated false-alarm rate.

This distinction is essential. Real patients and astronauts experience sensor errors, unexpected symptoms, environmental interference, and conditions not represented by a controlled simulator.

HELM's approach is to expose the testing process and make its assumptions inspectable, creating a foundation for future independent evaluation rather than asking users to accept unsupported performance claims.

9. Live NASA space-weather integration

HELM connects with NASA's DONKI space-weather API to retrieve information about solar events.

The interface clearly distinguishes live information from saved or offline data, avoiding the misleading impression that an old reading represents current conditions.

This is relevant because NASA identifies space radiation as a major hazard beyond Earth's protective magnetic field. Solar particle events can create sudden changes in radiation conditions, while galactic cosmic radiation presents longer-term exposure risks.

HELM provides environmental awareness that could support future mission decision-support workflows. It does not directly measure an astronaut's radiation dose or replace spacecraft radiation sensors.

Benefits and intended impact

HELM's central benefit is the possibility of gaining time: time to recognize deterioration, time to investigate a warning, and time to seek help before a situation becomes critical.

For astronauts, that means exploring a more self-sufficient approach to health monitoring during long missions with delayed communication.

For older adults, it means investigating whether inexpensive camera-based monitoring and personalized alerts can improve recognition of potentially dangerous events.

For healthcare teams, it means organizing multiple health signals into more understandable, traceable warnings rather than overwhelming users with isolated measurements.

For remote and underserved environments, it means developing health intelligence that can continue functioning without a reliable internet connection.

The economic motivation is significant. Older-adult falls alone represent an estimated $80 billion annual U.S. medical burden in 2020 dollars. Medicare already spends hundreds of millions annually on remote patient monitoring. These figures establish the scale of the problems and existing healthcare investment, not revenue projections or proven savings attributable to HELM.

HELM's future success would depend on demonstrating that it can identify meaningful problems accurately, avoid unnecessary alarms, improve response times, and integrate safely into real clinical workflows.

Tools, languages, and hardware

HELM's frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite.

Its testing infrastructure includes Vitest, with 103 automated tests, and Playwright for headless interface verification.

Core technical components include:

  • Personal reference intervals and conformal-prediction-inspired monitoring
  • Theil–Sen robust regression for trend forecasting
  • POS-algorithm remote photoplethysmography
  • Deterministic physiological-pattern matching
  • SHA-256 chained event records
  • Seeded mission simulation using mulberry32 pseudorandom generation and AR(1) noise
  • NASA DONKI space-weather integration
  • NASA Human Research Program countermeasure references

The current design prioritizes a standard laptop and built-in webcam rather than requiring a specialized diagnostic device.

This reduces prototype hardware requirements and supports the broader goal of accessible, locally operated health monitoring.

Future clinical deployment would likely require validated sensors, reliable monitoring coverage, secure notification infrastructure, and additional medical-device safety testing.

What makes HELM creative

HELM's most important innovation is not a single sensor or algorithm. It is the combination of several design principles into one system.

First, it focuses on change rather than isolated measurements. Personalized baselines and trend forecasting help users see how their health is evolving.

Second, it combines signals instead of treating them independently. The pattern engine considers how multiple physiological measurements change together.

Third, it is designed for environments where the cloud cannot be trusted to remain available. Monitoring and decision support operate locally, with external data clearly identified by connectivity status.

Fourth, it makes its evidence inspectable. Users can rerun simulations, inspect event records, and distinguish measured values from projections.

Finally, it connects an extreme engineering challenge with a widespread healthcare need. The constraints of deep-space medicine—limited equipment, delayed communication, and scarce medical expertise—also appear in remote communities and emergency-response settings on Earth.

HELM brings these requirements together in a working prototype designed to make health monitoring more proactive, understandable, and resilient.

Factors considered during development

The project prioritizes reliability, low hardware requirements, privacy, interpretability, and reproducibility.

The interface is designed to make important information understandable quickly, without requiring users to interpret complicated medical charts during an emergency.

Local processing reduces dependence on internet connectivity and limits unnecessary transmission of sensitive camera data.

Deterministic simulation makes it possible to repeat tests and inspect how the same algorithms behave under controlled conditions.

The project also separates established evidence from experimental results. Peer-reviewed performance from the earlier PPE-monitoring research is not presented as proof of HELM's clinical accuracy, and simulated emergencies are not treated as substitutes for real-world validation.

The long-term vision is to develop HELM into a clinically evaluated, offline-capable health intelligence platform that can support astronauts, older adults, remote workers, and people who cannot always reach medical professionals immediately.

HELM is built around one idea: the most useful medical warning is the one that arrives early enough to act on—and provides enough evidence to be trusted.
